what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, corpus, and base generator backbone; evaluate both on a shared ODQA suite under matched top-k budgets, reporting a unified bundle of EM/F1, abstention/selectivity rate, calibration, and latency/throughput. Crucially, harmonize the action policy by running each system in both always-answer and answer-or-abstain modes, so efficiency gains and sufficiency-aware selectivity are measured on comparable axes rather than against each other's native objective.

title_a: The LiveRAG Challenge at SIGIR 2025
title_b: Multi-Hop Paragraph Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
gold_rationale: Both works touch retrieval for QA, but they are structurally different artifacts. Paper A is a 2025 shared-task venue that fixes a web-scale corpus (Fineweb) and a specified LLM, soliciting heterogeneous end-to-end RAG submissions scored on overall answer quality. Paper B is a 2019 retrieval-method paper proposing a specific multi-hop paragraph retriever evaluated on Wikipedia-based multi-hop QA (e.g., HotpotQA) with retrieval-centric metrics. The role mismatch (challenge venue vs single method), corpus/domain mismatch, and metric scope (end-to-end RAG quality vs retrieval recall) prevent direct ranking, though both share the broad retrieval-for-QA failure family.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Submit Paper B's multi-hop retriever as a LiveRAG entry under the challenge's fixed corpus, generator, and evaluation harness, or conversely re-run LiveRAG top systems on a multi-hop Wikipedia benchmark with matched top-k and retrieval/end-to-end metrics. Comparability also requires harmonizing single-hop vs multi-hop query mixes and reporting both retrieval recall and answer-correctness on the same query set.

title_a: Backdoored Retrievers for Prompt Injection Attacks on Retrieval Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
title_b: Defense Against Prompt Injection Attack by Leveraging Attack Techniques
gold_rationale: Both papers touch prompt injection in LLM systems but occupy opposite roles in the attack-defense pipeline and cannot share a leaderboard as substitutable methods. Paper A is offensive, intervening at the retriever via supply-chain backdoor poisoning of a RAG pipeline and reporting attack success rate. Paper B is defensive, operating at generator/prompt-processing time and reporting defense effectiveness; it is not clearly RAG-specific. Threat models diverge: training-time adversary controlling the retriever versus inference-time injected-content adversary, so Paper B's defense is not necessarily designed for Paper A's backdoored-retriever vector. This mirrors the P08 attack-vs-defense asymmetry pattern.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Embed both works in a shared RAG attack-defense harness with fixed retriever, generator, corpus, and target queries; instantiate Paper A's backdoored retriever (with matched trigger and poisoning budget) as the adversary; evaluate Paper B's defense alongside other RAG defenses on the resulting pipeline; report a joint metric bundle covering attack success rate, clean accuracy, abstention/refusal rate, and defense effectiveness under matched threat-model conditions.

title_a: ADMIT: Few-shot Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on RAG-based Fact Checking
title_b: Hidden-in-Plain-Text: A Benchmark for Social-Web Indirect Prompt Injection in RAG
gold_rationale: Both works are attacker-side corpus injection studies on RAG and share the intervention point of writing adversarial content into the retrieval pool, so they live in the same broad threat family. However, the failure mechanisms differ sharply: ADMIT injects fabricated factual evidence to flip fact-checking verdicts (knowledge poisoning), while HiPT studies indirect prompt injection where hidden instructions hijack generator behavior via social-web text. Task scope (fact-checking vs general RAG QA), success metrics (verdict-flip rate vs injection compliance), and artifact role (method vs benchmark) also diverge, blocking a direct leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Build a unified corpus-injection harness with fixed retriever, generator, and matched insertion budgets, instantiating ADMIT as a knowledge-poisoning adversary and HiPT-style payloads as the prompt-injection adversary over both fact-checking and open-domain QA slices. Report a joint metric bundle covering attack success rate, verdict-flip rate, injection compliance, and clean-task accuracy, with explicit threat-model declarations for each attack family.

title_a: ProGRank: Probe-Gradient Reranking to Defend Dense-Retriever RAG from Corpus Poisoning
title_b: On the Vulnerability of Applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation within Knowledge-Intensive Application Domains
gold_rationale: Both papers occupy the corpus-poisoning/integrity space for RAG, so the failure family aligns. However, ProGRank is a defender that intervenes at reranking with a probe-gradient signal and reports defended answer correctness plus filter precision, while paper B is a vulnerability-analysis contribution scoped to knowledge-intensive application domains, likely reporting attack success rates and possibly domain-specific harm metrics. Role asymmetry (defense vs vulnerability characterization), domain scope mismatch, and divergent metric targets prevent direct leaderboard ranking, but a shared attack-defense harness is conceivable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Instantiate paper B's domain-specific attack vectors as the adversary within a fixed retriever-generator-corpus harness, then evaluate ProGRank as one of several defenses under matched insertion budgets and domain corpora. Report a joint metric bundle covering attack success rate, defended answer accuracy, abstention or filter precision, and clean-task utility, with at least one shared knowledge-intensive benchmark plus a general ODQA control.

title_a: Defending against Indirect Prompt Injection by Instruction Detection
title_b: A Few Words Can Distort Graphs: Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A is a defender-side contribution that detects embedded instructions in retrieved content to block indirect prompt injection on standard RAG, while Paper B is an offensive contribution that poisons the knowledge graph of GraphRAG to corrupt factual generation. The two works differ on role (defense vs attack), RAG architecture (text RAG vs graph RAG), threat mechanism (behavioral hijack via injected instructions vs factual corruption via poisoned triples/nodes), and headline metrics (detection accuracy and defense robustness vs attack success rate). They cannot be placed on a shared leaderboard as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe inside a shared attack-defense harness: fix a common RAG substrate (either both text-RAG or both graph-RAG), instantiate instruction-injection and knowledge-poisoning adversaries with matched insertion budgets, and evaluate Paper A's detector alongside graph-aware defenses against both attack families. Report a joint metric bundle covering attack success rate, detection precision/recall, clean accuracy, and abstention under a unified action policy.

title_a: Decide Then Retrieve: A Training-Free Framework with Uncertainty-Guided Triggering and Dual-Path Retrieval
title_b: Know Or Not: a library for evaluating out-of-knowledge base robustness
gold_rationale: Paper A is a training-free method that intervenes at the retrieval-trigger decision via uncertainty plus a dual-path retriever, targeting the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff of adaptive RAG. Paper B is an evaluation library (KnowOrNot) for out-of-knowledge-base robustness, i.e., whether a system correctly abstains on queries outside its KB. The failure foci differ (when-to-retrieve vs OOKB hallucination), the roles differ (method artifact vs benchmark harness), and action policies diverge (retrieve-or-not vs answer-or-abstain). They are thematically adjacent through uncertainty/knowledge-boundary reasoning but not directly rankable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Treat Paper A's framework as a system-under-test inside Paper B's KnowOrNot harness, holding backbone LLM and retrieval corpus fixed. Report a unified bundle covering OOKB abstention rate, correct-refusal, in-KB answer accuracy, and Paper A's retrieval-trigger rate, on shared in-KB and OOKB query partitions with matched prompting and a declared answer-vs-abstain contract.

title_a: Over-Searching in Search-Augmented Large Language Models
title_b: QuCo-RAG: Quantifying Uncertainty from the Pre-training Corpus for Dynamic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both papers address the adaptive-retrieval question in search/RAG-augmented LLMs, where unnecessary retrieval can hurt rather than help, so the failure-mode framing (retrieval is not always beneficial) and likely QA-accuracy headline metric are aligned. However, the interventions diverge: Paper A diagnoses and likely curbs over-searching as a behavior pattern in search-augmented systems, while QuCo-RAG installs a specific uncertainty-quantification signal derived from pre-training corpus statistics to gate dynamic retrieval. Action policies (when/whether to trigger search) and secondary metrics (over-search rate vs. retrieval-call efficiency vs. answer gain) are formulated differently, so direct leaderboard ranking is not warranted without harmonization.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, generator, corpus, and query distribution; evaluate both methods on a shared benchmark mixing parametric-sufficient and retrieval-necessary queries with ground-truth retrieval-need labels. Jointly report answer accuracy, retrieval-trigger rate, over-search rate, and accuracy on the no-retrieve slice under a common retrieve/abstain-from-retrieval action contract, ideally including QuCo's uncertainty signal evaluated on Paper A's over-searching diagnostic suite and vice versa.

title_a: When to Trust: A Causality-Aware Calibration Framework for Accurate Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
title_b: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
gold_rationale: Both works address the when-to-trust-versus-abstain failure mode in RAG and share an abstention/calibration-style action policy, so the problem family overlaps. However, the evidence modality diverges sharply: Paper A operates over a structured knowledge graph with a causality-aware calibration intervention, while Paper B targets unstructured contextual passages with an RL-trained grounded-response-and-abstention policy. Intervention paradigms (post-hoc calibration vs policy learning) and likely benchmark families (KGQA such as WebQSP/CWQ vs text ODQA) differ, so they cannot share a leaderboard despite the conceptual alignment on trust gating.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix a common evidence regime (either adapt GRACE to KG triples as context or apply the causal calibrator on text-RAG outputs) with shared retriever, generator backbone, and target-question set. Evaluate both under a unified action-policy contract reporting answer accuracy on the answered slice, abstention precision/recall or coverage-risk curves, and calibration metrics (ECE/AUROC) on matched benchmarks spanning the chosen modality.

title_a: Reliable Decision‑Making via Calibration‑Oriented Retrieval‑Augmented Generation
title_b: Sufficient Context: A New Lens on Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems
gold_rationale: Both papers sit in the trustworthy-RAG space where the system must avoid confident-but-wrong answers, and each likely supports some form of selective generation, so the failure mode and evidence assumption overlap meaningfully. However, Paper A intervenes on the generator to produce calibrated confidence and reports calibration-quality metrics (e.g., ECE/Brier, selective accuracy) alongside correctness, while Paper B proposes a diagnostic lens that stratifies queries by context sufficiency and likely reports accuracy and hallucination conditioned on that stratum. The action policies also diverge: confidence-threshold abstention versus sufficiency-conditioned answer/defer. Not a direct leaderboard match.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, generator backbone, and ODQA benchmark suite, then cross-evaluate Paper A's calibration method on Paper B's sufficient vs insufficient context slices; jointly report calibration metrics (ECE, Brier, selective accuracy at matched coverage) and sufficiency-stratified accuracy and hallucination rates under a single declared answer/abstain action policy applied to both systems.

title_a: PrismRAG: Boosting RAG Factuality with Distractor Resilience and Strategized Reasoning
title_b: The Curse of Helpfulness: Inverse Scaling Law in Robustness to Distractor Instructions via DistractionIF
gold_rationale: Both works share a distractor-robustness theme, but the operational definition of distractor diverges sharply. PrismRAG addresses distractor passages inside retrieved RAG context and intervenes at generator training to boost factuality, reporting RAG correctness metrics. DistractionIF targets distractor instructions injected into the prompt and is a diagnostic benchmark documenting an inverse scaling phenomenon in instruction-following robustness, not necessarily within a RAG pipeline. The intervention type (method vs benchmark), the locus of distraction (retrieved passage vs instruction), and the headline metric (factuality vs scaling curve on IF compliance) all differ.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Apply PrismRAG-trained generators to the DistractionIF instruction-distractor protocol while also evaluating DistractionIF-tested models on PrismRAG's RAG factuality benchmarks, using a shared model backbone family across scales. Report both RAG factuality under passage distractors and IF-compliance under instruction distractors, with a unified action policy covering answer, abstain, and ignore-distractor options.

title_a: Parallel Key-Value Cache Fusion for Position Invariant RAG
title_b: Beyond RAG vs. Long-Context: Learning Distraction-Aware Retrieval for Efficient Knowledge Grounding
gold_rationale: Both papers improve RAG generation quality and likely report answer correctness on overlapping ODQA benchmarks, so they share a problem family. However, Paper A targets position sensitivity (lost-in-the-middle) and intervenes at the generator via parallel KV-cache fusion to make outputs position-invariant, while Paper B targets distraction by irrelevant context and intervenes at the retriever by learning a distraction-aware selection policy (also engaging the RAG-vs-long-context efficiency axis). Different failure modes, different intervention points, and different action policies (order-invariant aggregation vs. selective retrieval) preclude a direct leaderboard ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the same base LLM and a shared benchmark suite (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA) with two controlled evaluation slices: a position-perturbation slice (gold passage placed at varied ranks) and a distraction slice (matched irrelevant-passage injection rates). Evaluate both methods under a common retrieval budget and action-policy contract, reporting EM/F1 per slice plus an efficiency metric (latency/tokens) so the KV-fusion and learned-retrieval interventions are compared on the same axes.

title_a: Entropy-Based Decoding for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
title_b: RAFT: Adapting Language Model to Domain Specific RAG
gold_rationale: Both papers target generator-side improvement of RAG quality under imperfect/distracting retrieved context, so the failure mode and evidence assumption broadly align. However, the intervention points are structurally different: Paper A is a training-free decoding-time method that reweights token probabilities via entropy signals, while RAFT is a supervised fine-tuning recipe that teaches the model to ignore distractors and cite oracle passages for domain-specific QA. Action policies differ accordingly (per-token decoding adjustment vs. learned distractor-aware generation), and RAFT's headline evaluation is domain-specific (PubMed, HotpotQA, Gorilla) while entropy decoding typically reports open-domain QA, so leaderboards rarely overlap cleanly.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the base LLM, retriever, and corpus; evaluate both methods on a shared benchmark suite spanning open-domain QA and at least one RAFT-style domain (e.g., PubMedQA, HotpotQA) with matched top-k and distractor ratios. Report EM/F1 plus a training-cost dimension so the training-free decoding intervention is compared fairly against the fine-tuned model, ideally including a stacked condition (RAFT model + entropy decoding) to test additivity.

title_a: Can Small Language Models Use What They Retrieve? An Empirical Study of Retrieval Utilization Across Model Scale
title_b: END: Early Noise Dropping for Efficient and Effective Context Denoising
gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic empirical study characterizing how retrieval utilization varies across model scale, with no proposed intervention and metrics oriented toward utilization/answer-correctness across model sizes. Paper B is a prescriptive method (END) that intervenes at context assembly by dropping noisy chunks early to improve efficiency and denoising effectiveness. They share the broad space of RAG under imperfect retrieved context, but the failure framing (general utilization vs. specifically noise) and the action policy (observe-and-report vs. filter-and-drop) diverge, so direct leaderboard placement is inappropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, corpus, and a matched suite of QA benchmarks with controlled noise ratios; evaluate END across the same small-to-large model scale ladder used by Paper A; report a joint metric bundle covering answer correctness, retrieval-utilization rate (Paper A style), and denoising efficiency/latency (Paper B style), so END's gains can be attributed across scales rather than only at one backbone size.

title_a: {MIRAGE}: A Metric-Intensive Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
title_b: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both papers contribute to RAG evaluation but produce different artifact types and cannot be placed on a single substitutable leaderboard. MIRAGE is a benchmark dataset with curated instances and prescribed, largely reference-based metrics spanning multiple evaluation dimensions, while RAGAs is a reference-free evaluation framework using LLM-as-judge to compute faithfulness, answer relevance, and context precision/recall over arbitrary RAG pipelines. They occupy complementary roles in the evaluation stack — substrate vs. metric methodology — so the comparison is partial rather than direct.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Apply RAGAs reference-free metrics on MIRAGE benchmark instances alongside MIRAGE's prescribed reference-based metrics over the same set of RAG pipelines with a fixed retriever and generator. Report correlation between the two metric families and their agreement with human judgments to assess whether they rank systems consistently across shared evaluation dimensions.

title_a: ReEval: Automatic Hallucination Evaluation for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models via Transferable Adversarial Attacks
title_b: Redefining Retrieval Evaluation in the Era of LLMs
gold_rationale: ReEval is a generator-side hallucination evaluation that synthesizes transferable adversarial perturbations of evidence to probe RALM faithfulness, reporting hallucination/answer-correctness rates under attacked contexts. Paper B redefines retrieval-side evaluation metrics so that retriever scores reflect downstream LLM utility rather than classic relevance. The two works target different pipeline components (generator behavior vs retriever metric design), assume different evidence regimes (adversarially perturbed vs naturally retrieved), and produce non-substitutable outputs, so they cannot be placed on a common leaderboard despite both sitting under the RAG-evaluation umbrella.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared end-to-end harness with fixed retriever, corpus, and generator where Paper B's LLM-utility-aware retrieval metrics are reported on ReEval-perturbed corpora alongside ReEval's hallucination rates, so each contribution is evaluated at its native pipeline stage within one protocol rather than ranked head-to-head.

title_a: MTRAG-UN: A Benchmark for Open Challenges in Multi-Turn RAG Conversations
title_b: RAGLAB: A Modular and Research-Oriented Unified Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both works are RAG infrastructure contributions but occupy non-substitutable roles: MTRAG-UN is a benchmark targeting multi-turn conversational RAG challenges (e.g., context carryover, unanswerability across turns), while RAGLAB is a modular framework for implementing and fairly comparing RAG methods, primarily on single-turn tasks. Their failure scopes diverge (multi-turn dialogue dynamics vs. cross-method reproducibility), intervention points differ (eval-set construction vs. framework/codebase), and they report fundamentally different metric bundles. They are complementary rather than competing, so direct leaderboard ranking is structurally inappropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe as integration rather than ranking: implement RAGLAB's catalog of RAG methods within its unified framework and evaluate them on MTRAG-UN's multi-turn protocol, reporting matched turn-level and conversation-level metrics (answer correctness, unanswerable detection, context-tracking) under a shared retriever/generator backbone. Symmetrically, audit whether RAGLAB's existing benchmark coverage subsumes or omits multi-turn challenges that MTRAG-UN isolates.

title_a: Generating Leakage-Free Benchmarks for Robust RAG Evaluation
title_b: Judge as A Judge: Improving the Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation through the Judge-Consistency of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Both papers contribute to RAG evaluation methodology and could in principle be combined in a single pipeline, so they share the broad problem family. However, they intervene at orthogonal stages: Paper A constructs leakage-free benchmarks to neutralize memorization shortcuts (data-side intervention, failure mode = test contamination), while Paper B improves LLM-as-judge reliability via judge-consistency mechanisms (scoring-side intervention, failure mode = unreliable evaluator). Their headline metrics differ (contamination/leakage diagnostics vs judge agreement and consistency), and their action artifacts are non-substitutable (a dataset vs a judging protocol), so direct leaderboard ranking is not meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Embed both contributions in a shared end-to-end RAG evaluation harness with a fixed retriever, generator, and target task; apply Paper A's leakage-free benchmark as the evaluation set while scoring with Paper B's judge-consistency protocol alongside baseline judges and human reference; report a unified bundle including memorization/leakage diagnostics, judge-human agreement, and downstream RAG accuracy so each method's incremental contribution to evaluation validity is isolable.

title_a: Whose Facts Win? LLM Source Preferences under Knowledge Conflicts
title_b: Rethinking All Evidence: Enhancing Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Conflict-Driven Summarization
gold_rationale: Both papers target the same failure family — knowledge conflicts between sources/evidence in LLM or RAG settings — so failure type and evidence assumption are broadly aligned. However, Paper A appears diagnostic, characterizing LLM source preferences under conflict without proposing a mitigation, while Paper B is a method paper intervening at context assembly via conflict-driven summarization to improve answer trustworthiness. The metric targets diverge (preference distributions vs answer correctness/faithfulness), and only Paper B has an action policy. They are in the same problem family but cannot be directly leaderboard-ranked.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Apply Paper B's conflict-driven summarization on the same conflicting-source instances Paper A uses to measure preferences, and report both source-preference shift (Paper A's diagnostic metric) and answer accuracy/faithfulness (Paper B's metric) under a fixed retriever, generator, and conflict construction protocol. Equivalently, evaluate Paper B's outputs through Paper A's source-preference taxonomy to test whether the intervention rebalances preferences toward the more reliable source.

title_a: Context-DPO: Aligning Language Models for Context-Faithfulness
title_b: FaithfulRAG: Fact-Level Conflict Modeling for Context-Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both papers target the same failure mode — context-unfaithfulness in RAG/LLMs when parametric knowledge conflicts with retrieved evidence — and share the assumption that retrieved context should be the authoritative source. They likely evaluate on overlapping knowledge-conflict benchmarks (e.g., ConFiQA-style stressors) with similar faithfulness/accuracy metrics. However, the intervention points diverge sharply: Context-DPO is a training-time preference alignment method that bakes faithfulness into model weights, while FaithfulRAG is an inference-time fact-level conflict modeling pipeline that operates on context representation without retraining. This makes them complementary rather than direct substitutes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the same base LLM backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2/3 or Qwen at matched scale) and evaluate both methods on a shared knowledge-conflict benchmark suite (ConFiQA, NQ-Swap, counterfactual context datasets) with identical context-injection protocols. Report a unified metric bundle covering context-faithfulness rate (or memorization ratio), answer accuracy under aligned vs. conflicting contexts, and computational cost (training vs. inference overhead) so the training-time vs. inference-time tradeoff is explicit.

title_a: Position: Retrieval-augmented systems can be dangerous medical communicators
title_b: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
gold_rationale: Paper A is a position paper arguing that retrieval-augmented medical communication poses pragmatic and safety harms in a high-stakes clinical domain, with no shared empirical protocol. Paper B is an empirical diagnostic of positional bias (the lost-in-the-middle U-curve) in general LLM long-context use, measured via multi-document QA accuracy and key-value retrieval by gold-document position. The artifact types differ (normative argument vs measurement study), the failure modes differ (domain-specific miscommunication harm vs position-conditioned retrieval accuracy), and there is no common metric, intervention, or action policy on which to rank them.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared empirical harness on medical RAG that operationalizes Paper A's safety concerns as measurable outcomes (clinician-rated appropriateness, hedging, omission of red-flag context) alongside Paper B's positional probes (gold-evidence index sweeps, distractor counts) on a unified medical QA corpus, fixed retriever and generator, and a joint metric bundle covering factual accuracy by position and safety-graded communication quality.

title_a: KnowPO: Knowledge-aware Preference Optimization for Controllable Knowledge Selection in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
title_b: Why So Gullible? Enhancing the Robustness of Retrieval-Augmented Models against Counterfactual Noise
gold_rationale: Both papers target situations where retrieved evidence conflicts with truth or with parametric knowledge, so the underlying failure family (counterfactual/conflicting retrieval) overlaps and both intervene on the generator. However, KnowPO frames the problem as controllable knowledge selection between parametric and retrieved sources via preference optimization (DPO-style training), while Why So Gullible frames it as noise robustness against counterfactual passages, with different intervention recipes and likely different action policies (selection vs resistance/rejection). Metric targets likely diverge: knowledge-source selection accuracy vs answer-correctness under injected counterfactual noise.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the retriever, generator backbone, and corpus; build a unified counterfactual-conflict benchmark that explicitly partitions cases by whether parametric knowledge is correct vs incorrect, with matched counterfactual injection rates; evaluate both KnowPO and the gullibility-mitigation method under a shared action-policy contract (use-retrieved vs use-parametric vs abstain) and report a joint metric bundle covering answer EM/F1, selection accuracy, and rejection rate on counterfactual slices.

title_a: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
title_b: RAG4GFM: Bridging Knowledge Gaps in Graph Foundation Models through Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Despite both titles invoking graphs and RAG, the two works tackle disjoint problems. Paper A is a hierarchical task planner that uses KG-RAG plus a symbolic verifier to produce executable plans, with failure modes around plan validity and metrics around task/plan success. Paper B augments graph foundation models with graph retrieval to fill knowledge gaps in node/edge/graph-level predictions, with failure modes around GFM generalization and metrics around graph ML accuracy. They share no common task, evaluation suite, or action contract, so a direct leaderboard ranking is structurally inappropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared knowledge-intensive graph task (e.g., KGQA or graph reasoning benchmark) where a KG-RAG-plus-verifier planner and a GFM-with-graph-retrieval system can each produce answers under matched retrievers, backbones, and graph corpora, evaluated with a common metric bundle (answer accuracy, faithfulness, and a unified abstention/action policy). Without such a shared task, only indirect qualitative comparison of design philosophies is meaningful.

title_a: Entity-Focused Dense Passage Retrieval for Outside-Knowledge Visual Question Answering
title_b: Quebec Automobile Insurance Question-Answering With Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A is an entity-focused dense passage retriever for multimodal Outside-Knowledge VQA, where the failure mode is retrieving entity-grounded knowledge for image-conditioned questions. Paper B is a domain application of RAG to French-language Quebec automobile insurance QA, where the failure mode is grounding answers in a specialized legal corpus. The modality gap (vision+text vs text-only legal documents), domain gap (open-world visual knowledge vs jurisdiction-specific statutes), and contribution type (retriever component vs end-to-end deployed RAG) leave only an abstract umbrella of retrieval-augmented QA, with no shared benchmark, corpus, or metric on which to place them.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Direct ranking is structurally inappropriate. Meaningful comparison would require collapsing them into a shared evaluation, e.g., both operating on the same OK-VQA benchmark with matched retriever/generator backbones, or both targeting the same text-only legal QA corpus with identical retrieval indices and answer-correctness metrics — neither is achievable without fundamentally redefining the scope of one paper.

title_a: Think-on-Graph 2.0: Deep and Faithful Large Language Model Reasoning with Knowledge-guided Retrieval Augmented Generation
title_b: ReFIR: Grounding Large Restoration Models with Retrieval Augmentation
gold_rationale: These papers share only the surface RAG label but operate in fundamentally different modalities and task families. Think-on-Graph 2.0 addresses multi-hop reasoning faithfulness in text-based LLM QA via knowledge-graph-guided retrieval, evaluated with QA correctness metrics over structured KG evidence. ReFIR addresses image restoration grounding via retrieval of visual references, evaluated with image-quality metrics like PSNR/SSIM/perceptual scores. The failure modes, evidence types, intervention pipelines, metric spaces, and output actions all diverge; no shared benchmark or substitutable method exists.
what_valid_comparison_requires: No reasonable harmonization is possible because the modalities (text QA reasoning vs. image restoration) and output spaces are disjoint. A valid comparison would require both methods to be instantiated on a shared task with a shared evidence type and metric, which is not feasible here without redefining either paper's contribution.

title_a: TRACE: Grounding Time Series in Context for Multimodal Embedding and Retrieval
title_b: Unified Generative and Discriminative Training for Multi-modal Large Language Models
gold_rationale: TRACE is a time-series retrieval/embedding system that grounds numerical sequences in textual context to produce multimodal embeddings for retrieval, whereas the second paper proposes a unified generative-plus-discriminative training recipe for vision-language MLLMs. They share only the loose multimodal keyword: modalities differ (time series plus text vs image plus text), failure types differ (retrieval grounding quality vs training-objective imbalance), interventions sit at different stages (embedding pipeline vs LLM training loss), and headline metrics differ (retrieval recall vs MLLM generation/understanding benchmarks). No shared leaderboard exists.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both methods to address the same multimodal task with overlapping modality pairs, a shared benchmark suite, and a common intervention surface; for example, instantiating the unified training recipe inside TRACE's retrieval setting over identical time-series-plus-text corpora with matched retrieval and downstream-QA metrics, or evaluating TRACE-style grounded embeddings within the MLLM benchmarks the second paper reports.

title_a: Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling
title_b: Context Tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both papers sit in the broader retrieval-augmented generation family but tackle structurally different problems. Chunk-Distilled LM is a model-side approach that retrieves and injects multi-token chunks into the LM decoding loop, with generation quality and efficiency (perplexity, throughput) as natural metrics. Context Tuning for RAG operates upstream on context/tool selection to improve downstream task performance (e.g., tool use, QA). The failure modes, intervention points, and evaluation conventions diverge enough that a direct leaderboard ranking is not meaningful, though both share the assumption that external chunks/context improve generation.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix a shared backbone LM, retriever, and chunk/context corpus, then evaluate both methods under a unified protocol that reports both LM-style metrics (perplexity on held-out text) and task-level metrics (QA EM/F1 or tool-selection accuracy) on the same benchmarks, with matched retrieval budgets and matched action policies (generation only vs. context-conditioned generation).

title_a: Cooperative Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Question Answering: Mutual Information Exchange and Ranking by Contrasting Layers
title_b: Separate the Wheat from the Chaff: Winnowing Down Divergent Views in Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both works are generator-side RAG enhancements for QA and likely share answer-correctness metrics on ODQA benchmarks, placing them in the same broad family. However, Paper A targets retriever-generator misalignment via cooperative mutual information exchange and contrastive-layer reranking, while Paper B targets a distinct failure mode of divergent or conflicting views among retrieved passages via a winnowing/filtering mechanism. The intervention points (cross-component cooperation plus reranking vs context filtering) and action policies (rank-then-answer vs filter-then-answer) differ, so a direct leaderboard comparison would conflate two non-equivalent problem framings.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, generator backbone, and corpus on shared ODQA benchmarks (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA) and additionally include a conflict-evidence slice (e.g., RGB counterfactual subset or ConflictQA) so both methods can be evaluated on benign and divergent-view conditions. Report EM/F1 plus a conflict-resolution metric and any abstention rate under a unified action-policy contract.

title_a: RankRAG: Unifying Context Ranking with Retrieval-Augmented Generation in LLMs
title_b: xRAG: Extreme Context Compression for Retrieval-augmented Generation with One Token
gold_rationale: Both works are RAG enhancement methods evaluated on overlapping ODQA benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA, etc.) with the same base LLM family, so they share a problem family and likely overlap on answer-accuracy reporting. However, the targeted failure modes diverge: RankRAG addresses retrieval quality by training the LLM to jointly rank and generate, intervening at the generator via instruction tuning, while xRAG addresses context-length cost by compressing retrieved passages into a single token embedding via a projector, intervening at the context-representation layer. The primary metric targets also differ (quality-centric vs efficiency-quality tradeoff), so a direct leaderboard ranking would conflate orthogonal objectives.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the retriever, base LLM backbone, and benchmark suite (NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, etc.), and jointly report a unified metric bundle covering answer quality (EM/F1) and efficiency (input tokens, FLOPs, latency) under matched context budgets. Ideally include a combined setting where xRAG compression feeds into a RankRAG-style ranker-generator to test orthogonality, and report per-context-length curves so quality and compression tradeoffs are directly visible.

title_a: SEER: Self-Aligned Evidence Extraction for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
title_b: Neuro-RIT: Neuron-Guided Instruction Tuning for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Language Model
gold_rationale: Both works are method contributions in the RAG quality and robustness space and almost certainly report answer-correctness on overlapping ODQA benchmarks, so they sit in the same problem family. However, the intervention points differ structurally: SEER inserts a self-aligned evidence extraction module between retriever and generator (filter and select), while Neuro-RIT performs neuron-guided instruction tuning on the generator itself. The implied failure framings also diverge — evidence selection and grounding vs general noise robustness — and the action policies (extract-then-generate vs robust-generate) are not substitutable on a single leaderboard. With only titles visible, finer alignment on datasets, noise protocol, and abstention behavior is not verifiable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever (e.g., DPR top-k from a common Wikipedia dump) and generator backbone, then evaluate both methods on a shared benchmark suite spanning clean ODQA (NQ, TriviaQA, WebQ) and explicit noise or distractor slices (e.g., RGB noise-ratio buckets, counterfactual passages). Report a unified metric bundle including EM/F1, abstention rate, and faithfulness or grounding under a declared common action-policy schema so extraction-style and tuning-style mitigations are scored on identical inputs.

title_a: Towards Secure Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Review of Threats, Defenses and Benchmarks
title_b: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
gold_rationale: Paper A is a comprehensive survey cataloguing security threats, defenses, and benchmarks for RAG, while Paper B is the foundational Lewis et al. RAG method paper introducing the architecture for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks evaluated on ODQA, fact verification, and generation under benign retrieval. The two occupy fundamentally different epistemic roles (secondary survey vs. primary method), address disjoint failure modes (adversarial integrity threats vs. task accuracy under benign retrieval), and share no evaluation protocol, metric, or action policy. They cannot be placed on a common leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Direct head-to-head comparison is structurally inappropriate; a survey and an original method paper are not substitutable artifacts. The only meaningful relationship is citational: Paper A should locate Paper B as the baseline RAG architecture against which the surveyed attacks and defenses are instantiated, then evaluate Paper B under a shared threat-model harness drawn from the survey taxonomy.

title_a: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Survey of Architectures, Enhancements, and Robustness Frontiers
title_b: LLM-Oriented Information Retrieval: A Denoising-First Perspective
gold_rationale: Paper A is a comprehensive survey synthesizing RAG architectures, enhancements, and robustness frontiers across the field, while Paper B is a focused denoising-first perspective on LLM-oriented IR. A broad survey and a narrower perspective or methodological proposal occupy structurally different roles and cannot be placed on a common leaderboard as substitutable artifacts. Even if both are non-empirical, the scope asymmetry (whole RAG field vs denoising subarea) and the absence of a shared evaluation protocol or metric target prevent direct comparison; at most, Paper A might cite or taxonomize Paper B.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either reframe both as method papers operating at the same intervention point (e.g., retrieval-side denoising for LLM consumption) evaluated on shared QA or IR benchmarks with matched retriever, generator, noise injection, and denoising-quality metrics, or recast the comparison as a coverage audit where Paper A's treatment of denoising-first IR is checked against Paper B's taxonomy. Direct leaderboard ranking is not appropriate.

title_a: Towards Trustworthy Retrieval Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
title_b: Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems: A Survey
gold_rationale: Both items are surveys with nearly identical scope — trustworthiness of RAG for LLMs — so failure family and evidence assumptions are tightly aligned and they likely cite overlapping literature on hallucination, robustness, privacy, fairness, and attribution. However, surveys do not propose interventions, do not report empirical metrics, and do not commit to an action policy, so there is no shared leaderboard on which to rank them. Comparability is therefore meaningful only at the taxonomy/coverage level, not as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Perform a coverage-and-taxonomy alignment: enumerate each survey's top-level trustworthiness dimensions (e.g., robustness, privacy, hallucination, fairness, attribution, safety), map cited works into a shared matrix, and report Jaccard-style coverage overlap per dimension plus divergences in framing, gap analyses, and recommended research agendas. Differences should be reported as scope/emphasis deltas, not as performance rankings.

title_a: Securing Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Taxonomy of Attacks, Defenses, and Future Directions
title_b: RAPID: Long-Context Inference with Retrieval-Augmented Speculative Decoding
gold_rationale: Paper A is a security survey/taxonomy cataloging attacks and defenses on RAG (integrity, privacy, availability threats), while Paper B is a systems-efficiency method using retrieval-augmented speculative decoding to accelerate long-context inference. The failure modes (adversarial corruption vs. decoding latency), assumptions (threat model vs. compute/latency budget), interventions (defense mechanisms vs. drafter-verifier speculative decoding), and metrics (attack success rate, defense robustness vs. tokens/sec, long-context accuracy) share no common axis. A survey-vs-method asymmetry compounds the mismatch — they cannot be ranked on any shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: No direct comparison is meaningful. The only legitimate cross-reference would be if Paper A's taxonomy explicitly classified speculative-decoding-style retrieval pipelines as a distinct attack surface, and Paper B reported a security evaluation (e.g., poisoning robustness of its drafter retrieval) on a shared threat-model benchmark — neither of which is in scope.

title_a: Trust or Abstain? A Self-Aware RAG Approach
title_b: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A is a defensive self-aware RAG method whose action policy is calibrated abstention, while Paper B is an offensive corpus-poisoning attack reporting attack success rate under an explicit adversarial threat model. The role asymmetry (defender artifact vs attacker artifact) and intervention-point divergence (generator-side trust/abstain vs corpus-side injection) preclude direct leaderboard ranking. However, abstention is a natural defense against retrieved misinformation, so the threat spaces meaningfully intersect and a shared attack-vs-defense harness is feasible, making this partial rather than invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Instantiate PoisonedRAG (black-box and white-box, plus adaptive variants aware of abstention) as the adversary with matched insertion budgets over a fixed retriever, generator, corpus, and target-query set; evaluate Trust-or-Abstain alongside defenses like RobustRAG and Astute RAG; report a joint suite of attack success rate, certified/empirical robust accuracy, clean accuracy, abstention rate, and abstention precision under a unified action-policy schema.

title_a: Magic Mushroom: A Customizable Benchmark for Fine-grained Analysis of Retrieval Noise Erosion in RAG Systems
title_b: Why Uncertainty Estimation Methods Fall Short in RAG: An Axiomatic Analysis
gold_rationale: Both works sit in the RAG diagnostics/reliability space but target structurally different failure modes. Paper A is a customizable benchmark that diagnoses how retrieval noise erodes answer quality, measured via answer correctness across noise types and ratios. Paper B is an axiomatic critique of uncertainty estimation methods in RAG, measured via UE-specific properties (calibration, sensitivity to context quality, abstention quality). The metric targets diverge (answer EM/F1 under noise slices vs UE soundness axioms), as do the action policies (answer-under-noise vs uncertainty-driven abstention), so they cannot be ranked on a shared leaderboard despite both being diagnostic tools.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Use Paper A's benchmark as the controlled stressor environment in which to evaluate the UE methods analyzed in Paper B, fixing the retriever, generator, and noise injection schedule. Report a joint bundle of answer correctness under each noise slice plus UE-quality metrics (calibration, AUROC for error detection, abstention precision/recall) so the two diagnostic axes are linked rather than competed.

title_a: Toward Robust RALMs: Revealing the Impact of Imperfect Retrieval on Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
title_b: RoseRAG: Robust Retrieval-augmented Generation with Small-scale LLMs via Margin-aware Preference Optimization
gold_rationale: Both papers address the same failure family — RALM degradation under imperfect or noisy retrieved evidence — and both ultimately concern answer correctness on open-domain QA, so they sit in the same problem space. However, Paper A is largely a diagnostic study revealing the impact of imperfect retrieval (with possible mitigation), while RoseRAG is a concrete training-side intervention using margin-aware preference optimization specifically tuned for small-scale LLMs. The model-scale assumption (small LLMs as a hard constraint vs general RALMs) and the intervention mechanism diverge, so they cannot be placed on a single leaderboard without harmonization.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the retriever, corpus, and a matched set of small-scale generator backbones; instantiate Paper A's mitigation (if any) and RoseRAG's margin-aware preference optimization on the same training budget and noise-injection protocol; evaluate on a shared benchmark suite (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA) partitioned by noise type (irrelevant, distracting, counterfactual) reporting EM/F1 plus any abstention rate under a unified action policy.

title_a: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
title_b: Supportiveness-based Knowledge Rewriting for Retrieval-augmented Language Modeling
gold_rationale: Paper A addresses complex task planning via Knowledge Graph-RAG with symbolic plan verification, while Paper B addresses supportiveness-based rewriting of retrieved unstructured passages for general RAG-LM. They diverge on failure type (plan validity vs unsupportive evidence), evidence modality (KG triples vs text passages), intervention point (hierarchical planner plus symbolic verifier vs post-retrieval rewriter), metric target (task or plan success vs QA correctness), and action policy (verified plan execution vs answer generation). They share only the broad RAG umbrella and cannot be placed on a common leaderboard as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix a single shared task family (e.g., complex multi-step QA or a planning benchmark) and a unified retriever-generator stack, then either instantiate B's supportiveness rewriter as a context-cleaning module inside A's KG-RAG planning pipeline and ablate it against A's symbolic verifier, or evaluate both on the same plan-correctness plus answer-accuracy metric bundle with matched abstention and verification-pass reporting.

title_a: Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems
title_b: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive contribution characterizing indirect prompt injection against deployed LLM systems with corpus/web-side attacker intervention and attack-success metrics, while Paper B is a defensive RL training method that teaches the generator to ground answers in evidence or abstain. The roles are structurally asymmetric and the evidence assumptions misalign: GRACE primarily targets natural evidence ambiguity and grounding, not adversarially crafted injection payloads, so they cannot share a leaderboard as substitutable methods even though both touch RAG robustness.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe as a shared attack-defense harness: fix retriever, generator, corpus, and target-query distribution; instantiate Paper A's indirect prompt injection as the adversary with matched insertion budgets and adaptive variants aware of grounding/abstention; evaluate GRACE alongside other defenses reporting joint attack success rate, clean accuracy, robust accuracy, and abstention/refusal rate under a common action-policy schema.

title_a: DRAGged into Conflicts: Detecting and Addressing Conflicting Sources in Search-Augmented LLMs
title_b: Rescuing the Unpoisoned: Efficient Defense against Knowledge Corruption Attacks on RAG Systems
gold_rationale: Both papers address problematic content in RAG retrieval and likely intervene at context assembly or generation, so they share a coarse problem family. However, Paper A targets naturally occurring inter-source disagreement (conflict detection and resolution under a benign threat model), while Paper B defends against adversarial knowledge corruption with an explicit attacker who writes malicious passages into the corpus. The failure types diverge (conflict vs poisoning), the evidence assumptions differ (no adversary vs bounded-budget adversary), and the metric targets are mismatched (conflict identification or resolution accuracy vs attack success rate reduction and clean accuracy). Pilot guidance explicitly flags this as not a direct ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Build a shared evaluation harness with a fixed retriever, generator, and corpus where both natural conflict slices and poisoning slices (varying injection budgets, black-box and white-box variants) are stressors run in parallel. Report a unified metric bundle covering conflict-detection F1, attack success rate, clean and robust accuracy, and abstention behavior under a common action-policy contract, so each method is scored on both threat models rather than only its native one.

title_a: RoseRAG: Robust Retrieval-augmented Generation with Small-scale LLMs via Margin-aware Preference Optimization
title_b: Faithfulness-Aware Uncertainty Quantification for Fact-Checking the Output of Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both papers sit in the trustworthy-RAG space but address structurally different failure modes with non-substitutable interventions. RoseRAG targets answer-quality degradation of small LLMs under noisy retrieval via generator-side margin-aware preference optimization, optimizing for correctness (EM/F1). The faithfulness UQ paper targets hallucination/unfaithfulness detection in RAG outputs via post-hoc uncertainty quantification, optimizing for detection calibration (e.g., AUROC). The action policies diverge (produce a better answer vs flag/abstain on unfaithful outputs), so they cannot share a single leaderboard, though they are complementary pipeline components.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, generator backbone, and a shared benchmark with both correctness labels and faithfulness/hallucination labels; evaluate both methods under a unified answer-plus-abstain action policy, jointly reporting EM/F1, faithfulness detection AUROC, and selective-accuracy/coverage curves. Ideally compose them (UQ as a gate over the preference-optimized generator) to test additivity rather than ranking them as substitutes.

title_a: Redefining Retrieval Evaluation in the Era of LLMs
title_b: Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling
gold_rationale: Paper A is a meta-methodological contribution that redefines retrieval evaluation metrics for the LLM consumption era, intervening at the evaluation-protocol level and targeting IR-style metrics recalibrated for downstream LLM utility. Paper B is an object-level language modeling architecture that uses chunk distillation to improve LM quality and efficiency, intervening at training and inference of the LM itself with perplexity or generation-quality metrics. The two works occupy different layers of the research stack and are not substitutable methods on any shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Direct head-to-head ranking is structurally inappropriate. The only meaningful bridge would be to instantiate Paper B's chunk retrieval or selection step as a retriever and score it under Paper A's proposed LLM-aware retrieval metrics on a shared corpus and query set, while separately reporting downstream LM-utility metrics. Without that reframing, no common evidence base exists.

title_a: LI-RAGE: Late Interaction Retrieval Augmented Generation with Explicit Signals for Open-Domain Table Question Answering
title_b: DSLR: Document Refinement with Sentence-Level Re-ranking and Reconstruction to Enhance Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: LI-RAGE targets open-domain table QA via late-interaction retrieval over structured tables with explicit matching signals, while DSLR refines retrieved free-text documents via sentence-level re-ranking and reconstruction for textual RAG. The evidence modality diverges (tables vs prose), the failure mode diverges (table retrieval and grounding vs noisy sentences in passages), the intervention points sit at different pipeline stages (retrieval scoring vs post-retrieval refinement), and benchmarks are non-overlapping (e.g., OTT-QA/NQ-Tables vs NQ/TriviaQA-style ODQA). No shared leaderboard or substitutability holds.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared harness with mixed-modality evidence (e.g., OTT-QA or a hybrid table+passage benchmark), fixed retriever and generator backbones, and a unified pipeline where retrieval-side late interaction with explicit signals and post-retrieval sentence refinement are ablated as interchangeable modules under matched EM/F1 and recall metrics.

title_a: TrustRAG: Enhancing Robustness and Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
title_b: SUGAR: Leveraging Contextual Confidence for Smarter Retrieval
gold_rationale: TrustRAG is a defense against adversarial corpus poisoning (integrity attacks), using clustering and self-assessment to filter malicious injected passages under an explicit threat model with attack success rate as the headline metric. SUGAR targets a benign efficiency problem, using contextual confidence to decide whether to retrieve at all, optimizing answer quality and retrieval-call reduction. They share only the RAG umbrella; failure mode, threat model, intervention point, action policy, and metric bundle all diverge, so they cannot be ranked as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Comparison would require collapsing them into a unified adaptive-and-robust RAG harness with both benign queries (where SUGAR-style skip-retrieval is meaningful) and poisoned corpora (where TrustRAG's defense applies), reporting clean accuracy, retrieval-call rate, and robust accuracy under matched attack budgets on shared retriever and generator backbones. Without a joint adversarial-plus-efficiency protocol, no direct head-to-head ranking is meaningful.

title_a: Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Revealing the Behavior of Large Language Models in Knowledge Conflicts
title_b: GraphRAG under Fire
gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic behavioral study of how standard LLMs/RAG resolve natural knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and provided context, measuring which source wins. Paper B is an offensive attack paper targeting GraphRAG architectures specifically via adversarial corpus or graph manipulation, reporting attack success. They diverge on retrieval architecture (text-based RAG vs graph-structured), threat model (benign conflict vs adversarial poisoning), role (diagnostic vs attacker), intervention point, and metric. No common leaderboard or ranking is structurally meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix a single retrieval architecture (either standard text RAG or GraphRAG) and a shared backbone LLM, then evaluate both phenomena inside one perturbation harness containing matched slices for natural parametric-vs-context conflict and for adversarial poisoning at equivalent insertion budgets. Report a joint metric bundle covering source-preference behavior, attack success rate, and clean accuracy under one declared action policy.

title_a: Adaptive Contrastive Decoding in Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Handling Noisy Contexts
title_b: Know Or Not: a library for evaluating out-of-knowledge base robustness
gold_rationale: Both papers sit in the robust-RAG family, but they target distinct failure modes: ACD handles noisy/irrelevant retrieved passages for in-KB questions via a generator-side decoding intervention, while Know-Or-Not is an evaluation library for out-of-knowledge-base queries where the correct behavior is abstention. The role asymmetry (method vs benchmark/library), divergent action policies (answer-under-noise vs abstain-when-OOKB), and differing headline metrics (answer correctness vs refusal/robustness) prevent a direct leaderboard ranking, though Know-Or-Not could plausibly host ACD as one system under test.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Instantiate ACD as a system within the Know-Or-Not harness on a fixed retriever and generator backbone, evaluate jointly on in-KB-noisy and OOKB partitions under a unified action-policy contract permitting abstention, and report a combined metric bundle including answer EM/F1, abstention precision/recall on OOKB, and over-refusal on answerable noisy queries.

title_a: Generating Leakage-Free Benchmarks for Robust RAG Evaluation
title_b: Superposition Prompting: Improving and Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A is a benchmark/evaluation contribution targeting train-test leakage as the failure mode, intervening at dataset construction to enable trustworthy robust-RAG evaluation. Paper B is a method contribution proposing a prompting technique that intervenes at inference to improve answer quality and reduce latency, with no engagement with leakage or noise robustness. The two sit in the RAG space but address orthogonal concerns: evaluation integrity vs. efficiency-aware prompting, with disjoint metrics (contamination/robustness deltas vs. accuracy and tokens-per-second) and no shared action policy. They are not directly rankable, though Paper B is in principle a candidate method to run on Paper A's benchmark.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Superposition Prompting alongside baseline RAG prompting strategies on the leakage-free benchmark from Paper A, using a fixed retriever and generator, and report a joint metric bundle covering answer correctness, contamination-controlled robustness deltas, and latency/throughput so the prompting method is evaluated under the benchmark's leakage-free protocol rather than treated as a peer artifact.

title_a: RAG-SR: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Neural Symbolic Regression
title_b: HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models
gold_rationale: These works share only the RAG acronym. RAG-SR applies retrieval to neural symbolic regression — searching mathematical expressions that fit numerical data, evaluated with regression metrics such as R-squared and MSE on equation-discovery benchmarks. HippoRAG is a neurobiologically inspired long-term memory architecture using a knowledge graph plus personalized PageRank for multi-hop QA over text corpora, evaluated with EM/F1. The failure modes (expression fitting vs multi-hop knowledge integration), evidence type (numerical samples vs text passages), intervention loci, metrics, and downstream actions are all disjoint, so no shared leaderboard is possible.
what_valid_comparison_requires: No direct comparison is feasible because the tasks live in different problem spaces. A valid comparison would require both methods to address the same task — either applying HippoRAG-style graph indexing to symbolic regression libraries with regression metrics, or applying RAG-SR machinery to text QA with EM/F1 — under a shared retriever, generator, and benchmark, which neither paper does.

title_a: Safeguarding RAG Pipelines with GMTP: A Gradient-based Masked Token Probability Method for Poisoned Document Detection
title_b: Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
gold_rationale: These papers share only the RAG umbrella term. Paper A is a defensive security mechanism that detects adversarially poisoned documents via gradient-based masked token probability under an explicit attacker threat model, with detection accuracy and robust QA as metrics. Paper B is a personalization system that builds editable memory graphs to ground a personal agent, evaluated on personalization/agent task quality with no adversarial component. There is no shared failure mode, no overlapping evidence assumption, no compatible intervention point, and no commensurable metric or action policy.
what_valid_comparison_requires: No protocol can make these directly comparable as substitutable methods. A meaningful comparison would require both works to address the same task (e.g., poisoning defense on personalized-memory RAG) with a shared threat model, shared retriever/generator backbone, shared corpus or memory store, and a unified metric bundle covering detection, robust answer correctness, and personalization quality.

title_a: Seeing through the Conflict: Transparent Knowledge Conflict Handling in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
title_b: Cordon-MAS: Defending RAG against Knowledge Poisoning via Information-Flow Control
gold_rationale: Both works are generator-side defensive interventions in the broader robust-RAG space, but the threat models diverge sharply. Paper A targets transparent handling of knowledge conflicts, which the literature typically frames as benign inconsistencies between parametric and retrieved evidence (or among retrieved passages). Paper B defends against adversarial knowledge poisoning via information-flow control in a multi-agent pipeline, presupposing an attacker with corpus write access. Natural conflict and poisoning rarely sit on a shared leaderboard; metrics (answer correctness/conflict disclosure vs attack success rate/robust accuracy) and action policies (flag-and-resolve vs quarantine-and-filter) are not directly substitutable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, generator, and corpus; evaluate both methods on a unified evidence-pathology suite that explicitly partitions natural inter-passage conflicts, parametric-vs-retrieval conflicts, and PoisonedRAG-style adversarial injections at matched budgets. Report a joint bundle covering clean accuracy, robust/conflict-slice accuracy, attack success rate, abstention/flagging rate, and any transparency-disclosure metric under a single declared action-policy contract.

title_a: Robust Fine-tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation against Retrieval Defects.
title_b: SeRTS: Self-Rewarding Tree Search for Biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both works aim to improve RAG end-task quality, but they target different problems with different mechanisms. Paper A is a generator-side robust fine-tuning method against retrieval defects (noise/irrelevant passages), treating retrieval as a fixed noisy channel. Paper B (SeRTS) intervenes at retrieval via self-rewarding tree search to improve evidence selection in the biomedical domain, not explicitly modeling adversarial or defective retrieval. Failure framing, intervention point, action policy, and domain/metric scope diverge, though both could plausibly co-exist as complementary RAG improvements.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever pool, generator backbone, and a shared biomedical QA benchmark (e.g., BioASQ/PubMedQA) with matched top-k; evaluate both methods under a unified protocol that reports retrieval quality (recall@k, evidence precision) and downstream answer correctness, plus a controlled noise-injection slice so Paper A's robustness claim and Paper B's search-quality claim are measured on the same axis. Ideally include an ablation combining tree-search retrieval with robust fine-tuning.

title_a: Detecting Hallucination and Coverage Errors in Retrieval Augmented Generation for Controversial Topics
title_b: Magic Mushroom: A Customizable Benchmark for Fine-grained Analysis of Retrieval Noise Erosion in RAG Systems
gold_rationale: Both works sit inside RAG evaluation, but they target different failure modes and play different roles. Paper A is a detection method for two output-side error types (hallucination and coverage) scoped to controversial topics where multi-perspective coverage is itself a first-class failure. Paper B is a customizable benchmark for input-side retrieval-noise erosion, measuring how perturbed retrieval degrades generation. Hallucination loosely overlaps with noise-induced errors, but coverage error and the controversial-topic scope have no analog in Magic Mushroom, and method-vs-benchmark plus detector-vs-degradation metrics block a direct leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's hallucination and coverage detectors as a defender on top of Magic Mushroom's controlled noise slices using a shared retriever and generator, reporting detection F1 per noise type and end-to-end answer quality. Symmetrically, extend Magic Mushroom with a controversial-topics partition and a coverage-error noise category so both papers report on a common failure taxonomy and metric bundle.

title_a: Retrieval augmented text-to-SQL generation for epidemiological question answering using electronic health records
title_b: Neuro-RIT: Neuron-Guided Instruction Tuning for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Language Model
gold_rationale: Paper A is a domain application that uses RAG to ground text-to-SQL generation over electronic health records for epidemiological queries, with success measured by SQL execution correctness against a structured EHR database. Paper B is a general RALM robustness method that uses neuron-guided instruction tuning to harden generators against noisy retrieval in open-domain QA. They share only the RAG label: failure mode, evidence corpus, intervention site, output modality (SQL vs natural-language answer), and metric family are all disjoint, leaving no common harness for ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared task and metric would be required, e.g., evaluating Neuro-RIT's neuron-guided instruction tuning on a text-to-SQL-over-EHR pipeline with matched retriever, schema, and execution-accuracy metric, or alternatively porting the EHR text-to-SQL system to an open-domain QA noise-robustness benchmark with answer-correctness scoring. Without one party crossing into the other's task, only indirect qualitative comparison is possible.

title_a: PR-Attack: Coordinated Prompt-RAG Attacks on Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Large Language Models via Bilevel Optimization
title_b: Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach
gold_rationale: PR-Attack is an offensive security contribution that crafts coordinated prompt and corpus-poisoning attacks via bilevel optimization under an adversarial threat model, reporting attack success rate. The second paper is a benign architectural study comparing RAG vs long-context LLMs and proposing a routing hybrid, reporting answer quality and efficiency on clean inputs with no threat model. Failure type (adversarial integrity violation vs benign accuracy/cost tradeoff), evidence assumptions, intervention points, metrics, and action policies all diverge; they cannot be placed on a common leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe as a shared attack-defense harness: fix retriever, generator backbone, corpus, and question set; instantiate PR-Attack as the adversary against the hybrid RAG/long-context router and against vanilla RAG and LC baselines; jointly report clean accuracy, attack success rate, and cost/latency under matched insertion budgets so the architectural choice is evaluated as a defense surface.

title_a: Beyond Black-Box Interventions: Latent Probing for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
title_b: FlippedRAG: Black-Box Opinion Manipulation Adversarial Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation Models
gold_rationale: Paper A is a defensive diagnostic that probes generator latent states to improve faithfulness under benign retrieval, while Paper B is an offensive black-box adversarial attack that manipulates opinions via retrieval-side corpus perturbation. The roles are structurally opposite (defender vs attacker), the failure modes diverge (natural unfaithfulness vs adversarial opinion shift), the threat models do not align (no adversary in A vs explicit black-box adversary in B), and the headline metrics are incommensurate (faithfulness vs attack success and opinion-flip rate). They cannot be placed on a common leaderboard as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe as a shared attack-vs-defense harness: fix retriever, generator, corpus, and target-query set; instantiate FlippedRAG as the adversary with matched insertion budgets; deploy latent probing as one defense among baselines; report attack success, opinion-shift, abstention, and clean-task faithfulness jointly under identical backbones.

title_a: Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling
title_b: Over-Searching in Search-Augmented Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Chunk-Distilled LM is a generation-side method that augments language modeling via chunk-level retrieval from a datastore, targeting fluency/efficiency and typically reporting perplexity or downstream generation quality. Over-Searching in Search-Augmented LLMs is a diagnostic analysis of when search-augmented LLMs issue excessive or unnecessary search calls, with metrics centered on search frequency, cost, and answer correctness trade-offs. The two works occupy different problem families: chunk-level LM augmentation versus search-decision policy. Failure modes, intervention loci, and metric targets do not align, so they are not substitutable on any shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared search-augmented QA harness with a fixed retriever/search tool, identical query distribution, and a unified metric bundle covering answer correctness, number of search calls, and latency. Both systems would need to be reframed as search-policy contributions (e.g., chunk-distillation as an alternative to issuing a search) and evaluated under matched search-budget regimes with an explicit answer-vs-search action policy.

title_a: Multilingual Retrieval Augmented Generation for Culturally-Sensitive Tasks: A Benchmark for Cross-lingual Robustness
title_b: Robust Fine-tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation against Retrieval Defects.
gold_rationale: Both papers sit under the broad umbrella of RAG robustness, but they target orthogonal failure axes. Paper A is a benchmark probing cross-lingual and cultural robustness in multilingual RAG, where the stressor is language/culture shift over culturally-sensitive queries. Paper B is a method paper that fine-tunes the generator to tolerate retrieval defects (noisy, irrelevant, or incorrect passages) in a largely monolingual setting. The failure types, evidence assumptions, intervention points (benchmark vs generator fine-tuning), and headline metrics do not align, so they cannot be ranked on a common leaderboard, though they are not adversarial roles either.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Extend Paper B's robust fine-tuning to a multilingual backbone and evaluate it on Paper A's cross-lingual culturally-sensitive benchmark, while also instantiating Paper A's stressors as a slice within a unified retrieval-defect taxonomy. Fix retriever, generator, and language coverage, and report a shared metric bundle covering cross-lingual answer quality, cultural appropriateness, and noise-slice robustness under matched protocols.

title_a: Unified Generative and Discriminative Training for Multi-modal Large Language Models
title_b: Accelerating Inference of Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Sparse Context Selection
gold_rationale: These papers occupy disjoint research areas with no shared task, modality, or evaluation surface. Paper A unifies generative and discriminative training objectives for multi-modal LLMs, targeting vision-language understanding and generation benchmarks. Paper B accelerates RAG inference via sparse context selection over retrieved text passages, targeting latency-accuracy tradeoffs on text QA. There is no common failure mode, no shared evidence assumption (multi-modal training data vs retrieved text context), no overlapping intervention point (training objective vs inference-time context pruning), and no comparable metric or action policy. Direct comparison is structurally inappropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: No protocol can make these directly comparable as substitutable methods. A valid comparison would require both works to address the same task (e.g., both targeting multi-modal RAG efficiency, or both targeting MLLM training under retrieved context) with shared backbones, datasets, and a unified metric bundle covering the contested axis.

title_a: CPA-RAG: Covert Poisoning Attacks on Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Large Language Models
title_b: Divide-Then-Align: Honest Alignment based on the Knowledge Boundary of RAG
gold_rationale: CPA-RAG is an offensive contribution that crafts covert poisoned passages injected into the corpus under an adversarial threat model, with attack success rate as the headline metric. Divide-Then-Align is an alignment method that trains the generator to respect its knowledge boundary (honest abstention vs answering) under benign retrieval, measured by answer correctness and honesty/abstention calibration. Failure modes (adversarial integrity vs benign overconfidence), threat models, intervention points (corpus injection vs generator alignment), and metric targets all diverge, so direct ranking is structurally inappropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe inside a shared attack-defense harness: instantiate CPA-RAG (and matched poisoning baselines) as the adversary against a fixed retriever/generator/corpus, then evaluate Divide-Then-Align alongside other honesty/robustness defenses on both poisoned and clean splits. Report a joint suite covering attack success rate, clean accuracy, robust accuracy, and abstention/honesty rates under a single declared action-policy schema.

title_a: Cutting Off the Head Ends the Conflict: A Mechanism for Interpreting and Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
title_b: A Few Words Can Distort Graphs: Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A is a defensive mechanistic-interpretability method that prunes attention heads in standard LMs to mitigate natural parametric-vs-context knowledge conflicts, while Paper B is an offensive corpus-side poisoning attack specifically targeting graph-based RAG architectures. The roles (defense vs attack), failure modes (benign conflict vs adversarial injection), evidence assumptions (no threat model vs explicit attacker), intervention points (generator internals vs knowledge graph), and metrics (conflict resolution accuracy vs attack success rate) all diverge. The system architectures also differ (standard LM context vs GraphRAG), making a leaderboard ranking structurally inappropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe as a shared attack-defense harness on a fixed GraphRAG stack: instantiate Paper B's graph poisoning as the adversary under a stated insertion budget, then evaluate Paper A's attention-head intervention (adapted to GraphRAG) alongside other defenses, reporting attack success rate, clean accuracy, robust accuracy, and abstention under matched threat-model assumptions and graph-structured evidence.

title_a: FiD-Light: Efficient and Effective Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
title_b: SURE-RAG: Sufficiency and Uncertainty-Aware Evidence Verification for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both works are generator-side RAG methods on knowledge-intensive tasks and could share QA benchmarks like NQ or KILT, but they target orthogonal objectives. FiD-Light addresses computational cost of Fusion-in-Decoder via encoder-output compression, reporting latency/throughput-quality tradeoffs under an always-answer policy. SURE-RAG addresses evidence sufficiency and uncertainty via a verification module enabling selective generation with abstention. They share no failure mode, intervention point, headline metric, or action-policy contract, so direct leaderboard ranking is structurally inappropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, base LM, and benchmark suite, then either compare on a shared answer-correctness axis under a matched always-answer policy with both efficiency and quality reported, or reframe along a single declared frontier (efficiency-quality Pareto or coverage-quality selective-prediction curve) where both systems are forced to expose the same operating points and abstention semantics.

title_a: The LiveRAG Challenge at SIGIR 2025
title_b: Multi-Hop Paragraph Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
gold_rationale: Paper A is a 2025 community challenge report describing a shared RAG evaluation venue with multiple participating systems, live/dynamic retrieval conditions, and challenge-defined scoring; Paper B is a self-contained method paper proposing a multi-hop paragraph retrieval algorithm evaluated on static multi-hop ODQA benchmarks (e.g., HotpotQA-style). They differ in role (venue/leaderboard vs single retriever method), intervention scope (whole-pipeline submissions vs retriever-only), failure focus (broad live-RAG failures vs multi-hop evidence chaining), and metric target. They cannot be placed on a common leaderboard as substitutable artifacts.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe comparability by entering the multi-hop retriever as one component of a LiveRAG-conformant pipeline (matched generator, corpus snapshot, query distribution, latency budget) and scoring it under the LiveRAG metric suite against other challenge submissions; symmetrically, evaluate top LiveRAG systems on a fixed multi-hop ODQA benchmark with retrieval-quality metrics (recall@k, chain recall) alongside answer EM/F1.
